main.title: Jak II
main.summary: Haven City's streets connect platforming missions, vehicle journeys and gunfights, while the music changes with Jak's actions.

cards.heading: The game
cards.text: Jak II is Naughty Dog's 2003 PlayStation 2 action-platform game and the sequel to Jak and Daxter: The Precursor Legacy. Known in Europe as Jak II: Renegade, it carries the pair through a portal into Haven City, where Baron Praxis rules behind fortified walls and experiments have given Jak dangerous Dark Eco powers.

cards.heading: Find a way through Haven City
cards.text: Haven City connects the adventure's missions through streets filled with traffic, pedestrians and guards. Jak can commandeer a zoomer to cross those districts, choosing between the road and the higher traffic lane as obstacles approach. An attack can bring the Krimzon Guard into pursuit, turning a journey to the next contact into another problem to escape. The city gives the story a place to return to: reaching an assignment means learning its streets as well as following the marker.

cards.heading: A gun between the jumps
cards.text: Jak keeps his double jump, punches and spinning attacks, then adds a Morph Gun with four weapon forms. A close group of enemies calls for a different shot from a distant target, and the gun can be worked into the movement between jumps. Ammunition gives those choices a limit. Dark Eco offers another response when enough has been collected, transforming Jak into a powerful close-range fighter. Familiar platforming controls now support encounters that can change quickly as enemies close the distance.

cards.heading: Music follows the action
cards.text: The soundtrack responds to what Jak is doing. A location provides a musical base, while drawing a weapon, riding a vehicle or using the JET-Board can introduce another layer. Composer Josh Mancell described building those parts so they could enter and leave without breaking the underlying piece. The result connects the sound to the player's change of pace: moving through an area and fighting through it can share a theme while giving the same surroundings a different energy.

main.title: Max Payne 2: The Fall of Max Payne
main.summary: Max Payne 2: The Fall of Max Payne is a 2003 third-person shooter game developed by Remedy Entertainment and published by Rockstar Games.

cards.heading: Max Payne 2: The Fall of Max Payne
cards.text: Max Payne 2: The Fall of Max Payne is a 2003 third-person shooter game developed by Remedy Entertainment and published by Rockstar Games. It is the sequel to 2001's Max Payne and the second game in the Max Payne series. Set two years after the events of the first game, the sequel finds Max Payne working again as a detective for the New York City Police Department (NYPD), while struggling with nightmares about his troubled past. After being unexpectedly reunited with contract killer Mona Sax, Max must work with her to resolve a conspiracy filled with death and betrayal, which will test where his true loyalties lie.

cards.heading: Bullet time and a noir love story
cards.text: Max Payne 2 is played from a third-person perspective. Throughout the single-player campaign, players mainly control Max, with Mona being playable in a few select levels. Both playable characters have access to a wide variety of weapons to eliminate enemies, as well as a bullet-time ability, which slows down time during combat. The bullet-time mechanic has been upgraded in the game to allow players to move faster as they kill more enemies, as well as reload weapons instantly. Due to the Havok physics engine being used, the game also features improved ragdoll physics. The story is again told mostly through graphic novel panels with voice-overs, although several traditional cutscenes are also used. Whereas the first game's plot was inspired by Norse mythology and traditional hard-boiled detective novels, the sequel is mostly based on tragic love stories like those seen in film noir, with Max and Mona's relationship being central to the game's narrative.

cards.heading: Acclaim, sales and a later sequel
cards.text: Max Payne 2 was released for Windows in October 2003, for the Xbox in November, and for the PlayStation 2 in December. The game received highly positive reviews from critics and, like its predecessor, has been cited as one of the greatest video games ever made. Praise focused on its action and story, while criticism targeted its short length. Despite the positive reception, the game sold poorly, leading Rockstar Games' parent company Take-Two Interactive to cite Max Payne 2's sales as a cause for the company's reforecast finances of 2004. Max Payne 2 received several industry awards, including Outstanding Art Direction at the Golden Satellite Awards 2004, and Editors' Choice Awards from GamePro, IGN, and GameSpy. A sequel, Max Payne 3, was released by Rockstar in May 2012. Remakes of Max Payne 1 & 2 are in development by Remedy and will be published by Rockstar for PlayStation 5, Windows, and Xbox Series X/S.

main.title: Crimson Skies: High Road to Revenge
main.summary: Nathan Zachary links dogfights, captured aircraft and a zeppelin home base across an alternative 1930s America.

cards.heading: Crimson Skies: High Road to Revenge
cards.text: Crimson Skies: High Road to Revenge is FASA Studio's 2003 Xbox aerial adventure, a new game in the Crimson Skies setting. Nathan Zachary leads the Fortune Hunters through an alternative 1930s America divided into rival territories. Compact fighter planes, airborne gangs and enormous zeppelins give its dogfights the scale and character of a pulp serial.

cards.heading: Keep the target ahead
cards.text: An enemy crossing the nose of the plane offers only a brief firing opportunity. Steering, rolling and using the throttle bring it back into view, while a special manoeuvre can reverse an awkward pursuit. Turbo helps close a gap but draws on a limited supply; braking can tighten an approach at the cost of speed. The controls let a single chase move between rapid repositioning and a short, controlled burst of gunfire, with the landscape close enough to become another obstacle.

cards.heading: A place to land
cards.text: A flight can end with Zachary stepping into an anti-aircraft gun, or acquiring another plane through an action prompt. These exchanges give the larger areas several ways to fight across them. A gun emplacement trades movement for a fixed view of the surrounding airspace; another aircraft changes which weapons are available on the next approach. Between story missions, exploring and taking on other work earns money that feeds back into the Fortune Hunters' growing collection of machines.

cards.heading: Choose the next aircraft
cards.text: Pandora, the Fortune Hunters' zeppelin, is both transport and home base. It gives Zachary somewhere to prepare the next mission, inspect the aircraft he has collected and spend resources on upgrades. Returning there turns money recovered during a flight into a practical choice for the next one. The different planes make that preparation visible: choosing another machine changes the shape on screen, its handling and the armament carried into the next dogfight.

main.title: Star Wars Rogue Squadron III: Rebel Strike
main.subtitle: Factor 5 · GameCube
main.summary: Star Wars Rogue Squadron III: Rebel Strike is Factor 5's GameCube action game expanding the Rebel pilots' campaign beyond aerial combat. Luke Skywalker and Wedge Antilles take part in missions across the original trilogy's setting, with spacecraft joined by ground vehicles and sections on foot. The player moves between different scales of the same conflict. An aircraft can provide a view over the battlefield before another sequence brings attention down to its machinery, soldiers and immediate obstacles, giving the familiar campaign a broader range of physical roles.

cards.heading: The squadron leaves the spacecraft
cards.text: Star Wars Rogue Squadron III: Rebel Strike is Factor 5's GameCube action game expanding the Rebel pilots' campaign beyond aerial combat. Luke Skywalker and Wedge Antilles take part in missions across the original trilogy's setting, with spacecraft joined by ground vehicles and sections on foot. The player moves between different scales of the same conflict. An aircraft can provide a view over the battlefield before another sequence brings attention down to its machinery, soldiers and immediate obstacles, giving the familiar campaign a broader range of physical roles.

cards.heading: Another vehicle changes the encounter
cards.text: The campaign introduces machines such as the AT-ST and speeder bike alongside returning starfighters. Each offers a different relationship to the terrain and opposing forces. The varied sections widen the idea of participating in a Star Wars battle, though their different controls and pace also make the experience less consistent than a campaign built entirely around flight. The strongest aerial encounters retain the series' clear connection between craft and objective, asking the player to recognise what must be protected or destroyed before chasing every enemy visible around it.

cards.heading: Bring a second pilot through Rogue Leader
cards.text: A cooperative mode recreates most missions from Rogue Leader for two players sharing a pool of lives. That substantial addition lets familiar operations be approached through coordination, with each person responsible for part of the larger fight. Competitive modes provide other ways to use the available ships. Unlockable Atari Star Wars arcade games connect the collection to earlier adaptations of the same films. Released in 2003, Rebel Strike's most durable expansion may be that opportunity to revisit a memorable flying campaign with another pilot beside the player.

main.title: SSX 3
main.summary: SSX 3 is a 2003 snowboarding video game developed by EA Canada and published by Electronic Arts under the EA Sports BIG label.

cards.heading: SSX 3
cards.text: SSX 3 is a 2003 snowboarding video game developed by EA Canada and published by Electronic Arts under the EA Sports BIG label. The third installment in the SSX series, it was released on October 21, 2003, for the PlayStation 2, Xbox, and GameCube, and was later ported to the Game Boy Advance by Visual Impact on November 11, 2003, and to the Gizmondo by Exient Entertainment on August 31, 2005, as a launch title.

cards.heading: Events across one mountain
cards.text: Set on a fictional mountain, the single-player mode follows snowboarders competing in the SSX Championship. Players choose from a variety of characters and take part in various events in different locations, earning points and money by performing tricks, winning races, completing goals, and finding collectables. Money can be used to upgrade character attributes, buy new clothes and boards, and unlock music and extras. Multiple players can play against each other in local multiplayer modes, and an online multiplayer mode also allowed players to connect to games and play against each other online on the PS2 version of the game, but it has since been discontinued.

cards.heading: Building snow and sound
cards.text: Development of SSX 3 initially began in 2001 following the release of SSX Tricky, the previous title in the series. The development team was composed of people from various different employment backgrounds, including an Oscar-nominated visual effects designer who worked as one of the game's art directors. The game includes thirty different types of snow and general visual improvements over the previous game, such as enhanced models and shadows. It was initially confirmed through a trailer in NBA Street Vol. 2 in 2003. A soundtrack album, SSX 3 Soundtrack, was released on September 30, 2003.

cards.heading: A million-selling action sports game
cards.text: SSX 3 was critically acclaimed, with reviewers praising the game's open world, trick system, presentation, and soundtrack. It was the first game in the SSX series to sell 1 million copies. IGN's Douglass C. Perry called it the best snowboarding game he had ever played, and GameSpot's Greg Kasavin recommended it not only to veterans but also for novices of the series. SSX 3 received the Academy of Interactive Arts and Sciences' awards for Console Action Sports Game of the Year and Outstanding Achievement in Licensed Soundtrack. Its 2018 re-release for Xbox One was also a success and was critically acclaimed.

main.title: Amped 2
main.subtitle: A mountain full of possible runs
main.summary: Amped 2 is a freestyle snowboarding game released for Xbox in North America on 28 October 2003. Its mountains offer space to link tricks, explore lines and build a reputation through a career. The player works towards score targets and performs for photographers positioned around each run, making a descent more than a race to the bottom. Developed by Salt Lake Games Studio, the sequel belongs to Microsoft's XSN Sports range. Its focus is the shape and control of a performance: where to take off, what to attempt and how to land.

cards.heading: A mountain full of possible runs
cards.text: Amped 2 is a freestyle snowboarding game released for Xbox in North America on 28 October 2003. Its mountains offer space to link tricks, explore lines and build a reputation through a career. The player works towards score targets and performs for photographers positioned around each run, making a descent more than a race to the bottom. Developed by Salt Lake Games Studio, the sequel belongs to Microsoft's XSN Sports range. Its focus is the shape and control of a performance: where to take off, what to attempt and how to land.

cards.heading: Make the trick look deliberate
cards.text: Completing challenges earns skill points that improve abilities such as spinning, jumping and balance. Progress therefore changes what the rider can attempt, while knowledge of a mountain reveals better places to use those abilities. Media objectives give a particular location a purpose: a trick has to happen where someone can see it. Events offer another route to fame and advancement. The player gradually moves from local rider towards professional recognition, learning to connect the terrain's opportunities with the requirements of an individual challenge instead of treating every jump as interchangeable.

cards.heading: Another way to ride the snow
cards.text: Snow skating adds a smaller board and a different set of possibilities beside conventional snowboarding. The roster includes professional riders such as Jeremy Jones, Torah Bright and Janna Meyen, linking the game to the sport beyond the console. Its licensed soundtrack supports the atmosphere of a filmed riding session, while XSN features connected performance to online competition and rankings. Amped 2 arrived between the original Xbox launch game and Amped 3 on Xbox 360. It develops the earlier game's interest in free riding through more challenges and a broader career.

main.title: Top Spin
main.summary: Top Spin is a 2003 tennis video game developed by Salt Lake Games Studio and PAM Development and published by Microsoft Game Studios for the Xbox in October 2003.

cards.text: Top Spin is a 2003 tennis video game developed by Salt Lake Games Studio and PAM Development and published by Microsoft Game Studios for the Xbox in October 2003. The game was later published by Atari Europe for Windows in 2004 and by 2K for the PlayStation 2 in 2005. It is a simulation tennis game in which players compete in singles and doubles tennis matches and exhibition tournaments. Gameplay modes include a career mode in which players develop skills and rise through the ranks of an international league. Top Spin featured an expanded control scheme compared to its contemporaries, and introduced several innovations including 'risk shots', in which players can execute more difficult serves and shots.

Top Spin was developed as a partnership between French company PAM Development and Microsoft Game Studio's Salt Lake subsidiary, with the aim of creating a more realistic and accessible simulation tennis game. The developers modelled the game on the design of previous console tennis titles including Virtua Tennis. Top Spin was developed to take advantage of the online capabilities of Xbox Live, with the game released as part of the XSN Sports brand and supported expanded online features.

Upon release, the Xbox version of Top Spin received universal acclaim by critics, with praise directed to the game's intuitive and accessible control scheme and graphical fidelity, with some critiques of the limitations of the game's career mode. The PlayStation 2 port of the game received mixed reviews, with attention directed to the reduced quality of the game's graphics. Following release, Top Spin received several sequels, with Top Spin 2 released in 2006.

main.title: Prince of Persia: The Sands of Time
main.summary: Prince of Persia: The Sands of Time is a 2003 action-adventure game developed by Ubisoft Montreal and published by Ubisoft.

cards.heading: Prince of Persia: The Sands of Time
cards.text: Prince of Persia: The Sands of Time is a 2003 action-adventure game developed by Ubisoft Montreal and published by Ubisoft. The game was released on the Game Boy Advance, PlayStation 2, GameCube, Xbox and Windows in November 2003. The Sands of Time is a reboot of the Prince of Persia series created by Jordan Mechner, who served as creative consultant, designer, and scenario writer for The Sands of Time.

cards.heading: The Dagger and the Prince's mistake
cards.text: The game follows an unnamed Prince whose father sacks an ancient city at the instigation of a traitorous Vizier. During the attack, the Prince obtains an artifact called the Dagger of Time, while his father's army captures an hourglass containing the mysterious Sands of Time. Visiting the palace of the Sultan of Azad to present the Sands as a gift, the Vizier tricks the Prince into releasing the Sands, transforming the people of Azad into savage monsters under his control. Together with Farah, a young Princess who knows the power of the Sands, the Prince works to correct his mistake and foil the Vizier's evil plans. The gameplay revolves around the Prince's platforming abilities, broken up by fights with the creatures created by the Sands. A key mechanic in the game is using the Dagger to rewind time if the Prince makes a mistake while platforming and use it to kill and freeze enemies.

cards.heading: Rewinding time becomes the guiding idea
cards.text: Concept work began in spring of 2001, after Ubisoft acquired the Prince of Persia catalog. After Mechner was brought on board, production began in June of that year. After the initial story draft was scrapped as it was too complex, the team began with four guiding concepts, including the ability to rewind time: this idea grew into the Dagger, the Sands, and the various powers related to them. Mechner's script drew inspiration from the Shahnameh, with the main focus on creating a simple narrative that worked with the pace of gameplay. The game used Ubisoft's Jade engine, originally designed for Beyond Good & Evil, another game published by the company. Production was troubled, with the team facing problems with the engine structure and delays with environment assets, while also managing to create an effective tester network to seek out the game's bugs. In 2004, a version for mobile phones was developed and published in North America by Gameloft.

cards.heading: A successful return for the series
cards.text: Upon release, The Sands of Time received critical acclaim, being nominated for and winning numerous awards and has been recognized by many as one of the greatest video games ever made. Sales were initially slow, but it eventually became a commercial success. A sequel, Prince of Persia: Warrior Within, was released in November 2004. Further games set in the Sands of Time continuity have been developed, and Sands of Time is generally cited as the reason for the Prince of Persia series' return to fame. As of 2014, the game has sold over 14 million copies worldwide, across all platforms. After several years of development, a remake of the game was cancelled in 2026.

main.title: Call of Duty
main.summary: Call of Duty is a 2003 first-person shooter game developed by Infinity Ward and published by Activision.

cards.heading: Call of Duty
cards.text: Call of Duty is a 2003 first-person shooter game developed by Infinity Ward and published by Activision. It is the first installment in the Call of Duty franchise, released on October 29, 2003, for Microsoft Windows. The game simulates infantry and combined arms warfare of World War II using a modified version of the id Tech 3 engine. Much of its theme and gameplay is similar to the Medal of Honor series; however, Call of Duty showcases multiple viewpoints staged in the American, British, and Soviet campaigns of World War II in Europe.

cards.heading: Allied soldiers share the battlefield
cards.text: The game introduced a new take on AI-controlled allies who support the player during missions and react to situational changes during gameplay. This led to a greater emphasis on squad-based play as opposed to the "lone wolf" approach often portrayed in earlier first-person shooter games. Much of Infinity Ward's development team consisted of members who helped develop Medal of Honor: Allied Assault. On release, the game received universal acclaim and won several Game of the Year awards. Retrospective assessments have been less favorable, with many critics saying the game aged poorly; it has placed low in lists ranking the series' games.

cards.heading: United Offensive and Call of Duty: Classic
cards.text: In September 2004, an expansion pack called Call of Duty: United Offensive, which was produced by Activision and developed by Gray Matter Studios and Pi Studios, was released. At the same time, the N-Gage version received an arena pack with three new levels. An enhanced port of Call of Duty for the PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360, titled Call of Duty: Classic, developed by Aspyr, was released worldwide in November 2009 with the release of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2, being available via redemption codes included with the "Hardened" and "Prestige" editions of the game.

main.title: SOCOM II U.S. Navy SEALs
main.subtitle: A squad returns to the field
main.summary: SOCOM II U.S. Navy SEALs is Zipper Interactive's PlayStation 2 tactical shooter, first released in North America on 4 November 2003. The sequel continues the combination of a command-led single-player campaign and online team competition. Twelve offline missions take the squad to Albania, Algeria, Brazil and Russia, giving each part of the campaign another setting and set of objectives. The player remains responsible for more than the next shot. Keeping the operation under control means deciding how the team should approach the area and what each order should accomplish.

cards.heading: A squad returns to the field
cards.text: SOCOM II U.S. Navy SEALs is Zipper Interactive's PlayStation 2 tactical shooter, first released in North America on 4 November 2003. The sequel continues the combination of a command-led single-player campaign and online team competition. Twelve offline missions take the squad to Albania, Algeria, Brazil and Russia, giving each part of the campaign another setting and set of objectives. The player remains responsible for more than the next shot. Keeping the operation under control means deciding how the team should approach the area and what each order should accomplish.

cards.heading: The next difficulty asks for a cleaner operation
cards.text: The campaign offers several ranks, with the harder settings unlocked by completing earlier requirements. Returning to a mission gives the player another chance to understand its approaches and use the squad more effectively. Objectives also unlock material such as music, concept art and multiplayer character models, providing smaller rewards beyond finishing the story. The tactical structure makes familiarity useful: knowing an enemy's position can change when the group moves and which route becomes safe. A better attempt begins before the first exchange, through a more informed plan for the team.

cards.heading: A regular meeting place on PlayStation 2
cards.text: Online competition became a major part of SOCOM II's identity, using voice communication to turn separate players into an organised team. David Sears returned as director, while Inon Zur composed the score. The European release followed in March 2004. The official servers closed in August 2012 together with other original SOCOM releases. Its importance belongs partly to the habits formed around it: arranging a match, recognising familiar teammates and using spoken information to make a shared decision. Those routines helped define what online console play could become during the PlayStation 2 years.
